query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of silicon into the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy promotes the formation of a stable, Si-enriched passivating oxide scale during high-temperature exposure in both oxidizing and reducing environments, thereby slowing degradation without disrupting the FCC matrix that underpins its strength and fatigue performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a single-phase FCC matrix showing notable strength and fatigue resistance.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a trace level of Si (e.g., 0.1–0.3 at.%) into the alloy composition during processing.
generation.conditions: Exposure to elevated temperatures (approximately 800–1200°C) under both oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres for controlled durations (e.g., up to 1000 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent, Si-rich oxide (such as SiO2 or silicate phases) on the alloy surface that acts as a passivation layer.
generation.mechanism: The added trace Si is expected to preferentially oxidize and form a dense, protective oxide film that limits further oxidation or reduction-induced degradation. This oxide scale minimizes reactive element diffusion and spallation without triggering phase transformations in the bulk FCC matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Si-modified alloy will show a thinner, more uniform, and adherent oxide layer with enhanced oxidation resistance. The integrity of the FCC matrix and mechanical properties (strength and fatigue performance) will be largely preserved during high-temperature gas exposure.
generation.baseline: The original Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy without Si, which under similar elevated-temperature conditions, forms less protective or uneven oxide scales possibly leading to accelerated degradation.
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 800–1200°C, exposure durations up to 1000 hours, and gas atmosphere conditions that are either oxidizing or reducing. The hypothesis applies only when processing maintains the FCC matrix and the Si addition is controlled at trace levels to avoid unwanted silicide phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise influence of the trace Si addition on long-term mechanical performance and microstructural stability remains to be quantified. There is uncertainty regarding the ideal amount of Si needed to maximize passivation while avoiding the formation of deleterious silicides.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of additively manufactured alloys: one set with the baseline composition (Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3) and another with an added 0.1–0.3 at.% Si. Expose both sets at a representative high temperature (e.g., 1000°C) under controlled oxidizing and reducing atmospheres for up to 1000 hours. Conduct pre- and post-exposure characterization.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology via SEM and EDS
Surface chemistry and phase identification through XPS and XRD
Mechanical property evaluation (tensile strength, fatigue testing) before and after exposure
Assessment of the oxide adhesion and continuity using cross-sectional microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si-added alloy does not develop a significantly more protective oxide layer (i.e., if the oxide scale is not thinner, more uniform, and composed predominantly of Si-rich phases) or if its mechanical properties degrade at a rate comparable to or worse than the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

These elements often contribute to passivation film formation, improving corrosion resistance. To enhance the mechanical properties of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), Si was added at varying concentrations (x = 0, 0.25, and 0.5) via vacuum induction levitation melting (re-melted six times for homogeneity). The microstructure and mechanical properties of NbMoTaWSix (x = 0, 0.25, and 0.5) RHEAs were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), universal testing, microhardness testing, and tribological equipment. Experimental results manifested that Si addition induces the formation of the (Nb,Ta)5Si3 phase, and the volume fraction of the silicide phase increases with higher Si content, which significantly improves the alloy’s strength and hardness but deteriorates its plasticity. Enhanced wear resistance with Si addition is attributed to improved hardness and oxidation resistance. Tribological tests confirm that Si3N4 counterfaces are optimal for evaluating RHEA wear mechanisms. This work can provide guidance for the fabrication of RHEAs with excellent performance.

reading.lever: Introduce a trace Si addition to form a stable passivating oxide without altering the FCC matrix.
reading.why: Si has been shown to enhance oxidation resistance via passivation in related HEAs, potentially addressing degradation without compromising strength or fatigue.
